**A floating-point system.** A floating-point system consists of a nonempty
finite set $\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb R$ of representable numbers with
$0\in\mathbb F$ and $-\mathbb F=\mathbb F$, a positive real
$N_{\max}\in\mathbb F$ (the largest normal magnitude), a positive real
$N_{\min}\in\mathbb F$ (the smallest normal magnitude), with
$N_{\min}\le N_{\max}$, and a rounding map
$\operatorname{fl}$ defined on $0$ and on the real numbers $t$ with
$N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$, taking values in $\mathbb F$ and satisfying
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$.

**Unit roundoff.** A real $u>0$ is a **unit roundoff** for the system when
every real $t$ with $N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$ satisfies

$$\operatorname{fl}(t)=t(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u,$$

with $|\cdot|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). The model quantifies all
subsequent error analysis through the single constant $u$ and says nothing
about the internal bit representation beyond the bound $|\delta|\le u$.

**The standard relative model.** For each operation
$\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$ and all $x,y\in\mathbb F$ such that $x\circ y$ is
zero or is a real number in the normal range
($N_{\min}\le|x\circ y|\le N_{\max}$; for $\div$ this includes $y\ne 0$), the
computed result is

$$\operatorname{fl}(x\circ y)=(x\circ y)(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u.$$

When $x\circ y=0$, this identity is the exact-zero rule
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$ and one may take $\delta=0$.

**The exclusions are part of the model, and are stated explicitly.**

- **Overflow** is excluded: when $|x\circ y|>N_{\max}$ the result is not a real
  number of the form $(x\circ y)(1+\delta)$ with $|\delta|\le u$.
- **Underflow** is excluded: when $0<|x\circ y|<N_{\min}$ the result falls into
  the subnormal or lost range and need not satisfy the relative bound.
- **Invalid operations** are excluded: when $x\circ y$ is not a real number
  (for example $0/0$), there is no real $\delta$ for the displayed identity.

Every item on this page that uses the model therefore carries the hypotheses
that the relevant operations lie in the normal range, and statements about
overflow, underflow or invalid operations are made only where the exclusion is
mentioned.

These coordinate assignments are available because the $z_{i,j}$ are independent variables.

In every orientation determinant each coordinate increment has degree at most one. In a lifted determinant it has degree at most two, because it can occur squared in one lifted entry and a determinant term selects only one entry from that row. Thus every monomial exponent vector has digits $a_k\in\{0,1,2\}$. Under the substitution in [F2], its $\varepsilon$ exponent is $\sum_k a_k3^k$. Uniqueness of base-three expansion makes this map injective, so distinct monomials cannot merge or cancel. The nonzero polynomial from [step 1.1] remains nonzero after substitution.

Write any resulting polynomial as $P(\varepsilon)=c_m\varepsilon^m+\sum_{j>m}c_j\varepsilon^j$, with $c_m\ne0$. If $B=\sum_{j>m}|c_j|$ is positive, then for $0<\varepsilon<\min(1,|c_m|/(2B))$ the tail after dividing by $\varepsilon^m$ has absolute value at most $\varepsilon B<|c_m|/2$ by [F5] and [F6]. If $B=0$, its sign is already constant. In either case the sign for sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$ is the sign of $c_m$. If the original determinant is nonzero, its constant coefficient is nonzero and is the first coefficient, so its sign is preserved.

A finite point set has only finitely many ordered orientation and lifted predicate tuples. For each resulting polynomial with tail bound $B>0$ in [step 3.1], form its positive threshold $t_P=\min(1,|c_m|/(2B))$. Every remaining polynomial has $B=0$, so it is a single nonzero monomial and has its first-coefficient sign for every $\varepsilon>0$. **A floating-point system.** A floating-point system consists of a nonempty
finite set $\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb R$ of representable numbers with
$0\in\mathbb F$ and $-\mathbb F=\mathbb F$, a positive real
$N_{\max}\in\mathbb F$ (the largest normal magnitude), a positive real
$N_{\min}\in\mathbb F$ (the smallest normal magnitude), with
$N_{\min}\le N_{\max}$, and a rounding map
$\operatorname{fl}$ defined on $0$ and on the real numbers $t$ with
$N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$, taking values in $\mathbb F$ and satisfying
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$.

**Unit roundoff.** A real $u>0$ is a **unit roundoff** for the system when
every real $t$ with $N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$ satisfies

$$\operatorname{fl}(t)=t(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u,$$

with $|\cdot|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). The model quantifies all
subsequent error analysis through the single constant $u$ and says nothing
about the internal bit representation beyond the bound $|\delta|\le u$.

**The standard relative model.** For each operation
$\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$ and all $x,y\in\mathbb F$ such that $x\circ y$ is
zero or is a real number in the normal range
($N_{\min}\le|x\circ y|\le N_{\max}$; for $\div$ this includes $y\ne 0$), the
computed result is

$$\operatorname{fl}(x\circ y)=(x\circ y)(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u.$$

When $x\circ y=0$, this identity is the exact-zero rule
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$ and one may take $\delta=0$.

- **Overflow** is excluded: when $|x\circ y|>N_{\max}$ the result is not a real
  number of the form $(x\circ y)(1+\delta)$ with $|\delta|\le u$.
- **Underflow** is excluded: when $0<|x\circ y|<N_{\min}$ the result falls into
  the subnormal or lost range and need not satisfy the relative bound.
- **Invalid operations** are excluded: when $x\circ y$ is not a real number
  (for example $0/0$), there is no real $\delta$ for the displayed identity.

Every item on this page that uses the model therefore carries the hypotheses
that the relevant operations lie in the normal range, and statements about
overflow, underflow or invalid operations are made only where the exclusion is
mentioned.

integer $s\ge1$ and a square matrix $M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<s}$ over $\mathbb D$, define
$$
\det M=\sum_{\pi\in S_s}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=0}^{s-1}M_{i,\pi(i)},
$$
where $S_s$ is the set of permutations of $\{0,\ldots,s-1\}$ and
$\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}$ with
$\operatorname{inv}(\pi)=\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}$.

$\operatorname{sgn}(x)=+1$ for $x>0$, $0$ for $x=0$, and $-1$ for $x<0$. For ordered points

$(p_i,\sum_{j=1}^d p_{i,j}^2,1)$ and put $L_d=\det K_d$. The raw incircle

then squared norm, then $1$. If $O_d\ne0$, define the orientation-normalized

**A floating-point system.** A floating-point system consists of a nonempty
finite set $\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb R$ of representable numbers with
$0\in\mathbb F$ and $-\mathbb F=\mathbb F$, a positive real
$N_{\max}\in\mathbb F$ (the largest normal magnitude), a positive real
$N_{\min}\in\mathbb F$ (the smallest normal magnitude), with
$N_{\min}\le N_{\max}$, and a rounding map
$\operatorname{fl}$ defined on $0$ and on the real numbers $t$ with
$N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$, taking values in $\mathbb F$ and satisfying
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$.

**Unit roundoff.** A real $u>0$ is a **unit roundoff** for the system when
every real $t$ with $N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$ satisfies

$$\operatorname{fl}(t)=t(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u,$$

with $|\cdot|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). The model quantifies all
subsequent error analysis through the single constant $u$ and says nothing
about the internal bit representation beyond the bound $|\delta|\le u$.

**The standard relative model.** For each operation
$\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$ and all $x,y\in\mathbb F$ such that $x\circ y$ is
zero or is a real number in the normal range
($N_{\min}\le|x\circ y|\le N_{\max}$; for $\div$ this includes $y\ne 0$), the
computed result is

$$\operatorname{fl}(x\circ y)=(x\circ y)(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u.$$

When $x\circ y=0$, this identity is the exact-zero rule
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$ and one may take $\delta=0$.

**The exclusions are part of the model, and are stated explicitly.**

- **Overflow** is excluded: when $|x\circ y|>N_{\max}$ the result is not a real
  number of the form $(x\circ y)(1+\delta)$ with $|\delta|\le u$.
- **Underflow** is excluded: when $0<|x\circ y|<N_{\min}$ the result falls into
  the subnormal or lost range and need not satisfy the relative bound.
- **Invalid operations** are excluded: when $x\circ y$ is not a real number
  (for example $0/0$), there is no real $\delta$ for the displayed identity.

Every item on this page that uses the model therefore carries the hypotheses
that the relevant operations lie in the normal range, and statements about
overflow, underflow or invalid operations are made only where the exclusion is
mentioned.

Let $M$ be an $s\times s$ matrix, $s\ge2$, whose entries are exactly represented in a
selected floating-point system. Compute its Leibniz determinant by forming each
product left-to-right, applying each permutation sign by an exact sign-bit
change, and summing the $s!$ signed terms left-to-right. If every
rounded operation is zero or has a normal-range exact result, every operation
satisfies the standard relative model with unit roundoff $u$, and
$qu<1$ for $q=s+s!-2$, then
$$|\widehat D-\det M|\le \gamma_q S,\qquad \gamma_q=\frac{qu}{1-qu},\qquad S=\sum_{\pi\in S_s}\prod_{i=0}^{s-1}|M_{i,\pi(i)}|.$$

An exact dyadic rational is a number $m2^q$ with integers $m,q$.
Fix integers $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$ and
$N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{e_{\max}-p+1}$. The finite representable set $\mathbb F$
consists of zero, both signs of every normal number $k2^{e-p+1}$ with integers $e,k$ satisfying
$e_{\min}\le e\le e_{\max}$ and $2^{p-1}\le k<2^p$, and both signs of every
subnormal number $k\eta$ with integer $k$ satisfying $1\le k<2^{p-1}$. The smallest positive
subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains
$-\infty$ and $+\infty$ as enclosure sentinels; they are not finite machine
numbers.

For a real $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, define $\operatorname{rd}(x)$ as the
greatest member of $\mathbb F$ not exceeding $x$, and $\operatorname{ru}(x)$ as
the least member of $\mathbb F$ not less than $x$. Define
$\rho(x)=\operatorname{ru}(x)-\operatorname{rd}(x)$. Set $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(0)=0$.
For nonzero $x$ in the
subnormal range, define the absolute-error bound $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=\eta$;
for $2^e\le |x|<2^{e+1}$ in the normal range, define
$\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=2^{e-p+2}$. For $x>N_{\max}$, set
$(\operatorname{rd}(x),\operatorname{ru}(x))=(N_{\max},+\infty)$; for
$x<-N_{\max}$, set
$(\operatorname{rd}(x),\operatorname{ru}(x))=(-\infty,-N_{\max})$.
In either overflow case set $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=+\infty$ and report
`overflow`, even when the selected directed endpoint is finite.
The rounding procedure reports `finite`, `subnormal`, or
`overflow`, so no relative-error assumption is implicit.

An exact rational intermediate may be converted by comparing integer
numerators and denominators after clearing powers of two. A directed interval
endpoint is the resulting greatest lower or least upper member of the
extended endpoint set $\mathbb F\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$.

For finite $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, the directed roundings defined in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]] satisfy
$\operatorname{rd}(x)\le x\le\operatorname{ru}(x)$ and each endpoint error is
at most the stated $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)$ (with zero error when $x$ is
representable). For $x>N_{\max}$ the pair $(N_{\max},+\infty)$ encloses $x$;
for $x<-N_{\max}$ the pair $(-\infty,-N_{\max})$ encloses $x$. Overflow has
error bound $+\infty$ and cannot be reported as a finite-error result.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in

from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node

node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

derivations.claim: Each finitely encoded dyadic entry can be put in the form in [F1] by integer shifts and cancellation of powers of two; zero uses exponent zero. Since $s\ge1$, every row has a nonempty finite list of exponents and its maximum $k_i$ exists and is computed by finitely many comparisons. Then $N_{ij}=a_{ij}2^{k_i-b_{ij}}$ is an exactly computable integer.

In each permutation product of $N$, the row factors multiply to the same positive integer $C=\prod_i2^{k_i}$. Thus [F2] gives $\det N=C\det M$, the sign-preserving identity underlying [F3]. The integer sum in [F1] is exactly $\det N$, so the returned sign equals $\operatorname{sgn}(\det M)$, also when this value is zero.

There are exactly $s!$ permutations, which can be enumerated in lexicographic order from the finite set of tuples of length $s$ with entries in $\{0,\ldots,s-1\}$ by retaining those with distinct entries. Each product, sum, integer shift and sign comparison operates on finite integer encodings and terminates. Hence all loops and the algorithm terminate, even for singular matrices and $s=1$; there is no pivot division. All constructions are explicit and finite, so no axiom of choice is used.
